note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Biology board exam 2024, Q.P. code 57/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Figures are described in words. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In which of the following plants are both male and female flowers borne on the same plant, so that pollination can be geitonogamy or xenogamy?
questions.solution: Maize is monoecious, so autogamy is prevented but geitonogamy and xenogamy are possible. Papaya, date palm and spinach are dioecious.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which one of the following hormones is secreted by the human placenta and helps in the maintenance of pregnancy?
questions.solution: hCG maintains the corpus luteum, which keeps secreting progesterone for the pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The periodic abstinence by a couple for family planning should be from :
options: Day 5 to 10 of the menstrual cycle
Day 13 to 15 of the menstrual cycle
Day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle
Day 16 to 20 of the menstrual cycle
questions.solution: Ovulation is expected around day 14, so the fertile period is roughly day 10 to 17.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Select the incorrect match of human karyotype and characters :
options: 45 + XX – broad palm with characteristic palm crease
44 + XO – sterile females as ovaries are rudimentary
questions.solution: Klinefelter's syndrome (44 + XXY) shows overall masculine development with some feminine features such as gynaecomastia.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: There are 20 amino acids and 4 bases in DNA, and a combination of 3 bases codes for an amino acid. If instead there were 96 different amino acids and 12 different bases, the minimum number of bases required to form a codon would be :
questions.solution: 12¹ = 12 is too few, but 12² = 144 combinations cover 96 amino acids, so 2 bases are enough.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a schematic polynucleotide chain drawn as phosphate (P) and sugar (S) units alternating along the backbone, with each sugar joined to a base (B) by a dotted line, the dotted line S – – – B represents :
questions.solution: The base is attached to the 1′ carbon of the sugar by an N-glycosidic linkage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is there a substantial increase in the activity of mast cells in the human body?
questions.solution: In allergy, mast cells release chemicals such as histamine and serotonin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Lactobacillus, which sets milk into curd, is categorised as :
questions.solution: Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria) is heterotrophic.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which one of the following transgenic animals is being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine?
questions.solution: Transgenic mice are used to test the safety of polio vaccine before human use.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The restriction endonuclease Hind II always cuts DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of :
questions.solution: Hind II recognises a specific six-base-pair sequence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The improved trait found in the genetically modified crop Golden rice is :
questions.solution: Golden rice is rich in β-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers, and the biomass available for consumption by herbivores and decomposers, are referred to as :
options: Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity
Net primary productivity and secondary productivity
Secondary productivity and net primary productivity
Secondary productivity and gross primary productivity
questions.solution: Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers; NPP is the biomass available to herbivores and decomposers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The laws of our country permit legal adoption and it is as yet one of the best methods for childless couples looking for parenthood.
Reason (R): Emotional, religious and social factors are no deterrents to the legal adoption of orphaned and destitute children in India.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Emotional, religious and social factors are in fact deterrents to adoption, so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Linked genes do not show the dihybrid F₂ ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Reason (R): Linked genes do not undergo independent assortment.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The 9:3:3:1 ratio depends on independent assortment, which linked genes do not show.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a pathogen of several monocot plants.
Reason (R): It is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as T-DNA to transform normal plant cells into a tumour.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Agrobacterium tumefaciens infects dicot plants, so A is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The Indian Government has set up an organisation known as GEAC to decide the validity of GM research.
Reason (R): Genetic modification of organisms has no effect when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: GEAC exists precisely because GM organisms can have unpredictable effects, so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Identify A, B, C and D : Pericarp – A; B – cotyledon in seed of grass family; Embryonal axis – C; D – remains of nucellus in a seed.
questions.solution: A: wall of the fruit (developed from the ovary wall). B: scutellum. C: the plumule and radicle (the axis that forms the future shoot and root). D: perisperm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A picture shows a series of giraffes, from short-necked ones grazing on the ground to long-necked ones reaching leaves high on tall trees, as if stretching their necks over generations. Name the naturalist and write the explanation given by him that evolution had occurred on this basis.
questions.solution: Lamarck. He proposed that evolution occurs by the use and disuse of organs: ancestors of giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves on tall trees, the neck gradually lengthened, and this acquired character was passed on to the next generations (inheritance of acquired characters).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Write the basic steps followed in the assisted reproductive technologies (ART) programme to help childless couples. Why is it also known as the test tube baby programme?
questions.solution: Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and made to fuse in the laboratory under conditions similar to the body (in vitro fertilisation). The zygote or early embryo is transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT, up to 8 blastomeres) or uterus (IUT, more than 8 blastomeres) to develop further. It is called the test tube baby programme because fertilisation takes place outside the body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A farmer working on his farm was bitten by a poisonous snake. He was rushed to a nearby health centre where the doctor gave him an injection to save his life. (i) What did the doctor inject and why? (ii) Name the kind of immunity provided by this injection.
questions.solution: (i) Antivenom (anti-venom serum), which contains preformed antibodies against the snake venom and acts quickly to neutralise it. (ii) Passive immunity (artificially acquired).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Why do organic farmers not recommend complete eradication of insect pests? Explain giving reason.
questions.solution: Organic farmers aim to keep pests at manageable levels. Beneficial predatory and parasitic insects depend on the pests for food, so eradicating pests would also eliminate these useful organisms and upset the ecological balance and food webs of the farm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A pyramid of biomass is shown in which the primary consumer level A (PC) is wider than the primary producer level B (PP) below it. Name the two standing crops that could occupy levels A and B. Name this type of pyramid and the ecosystem in which it is found.
questions.solution: A: small fish or zooplankton (primary consumers); B: phytoplankton (producers). It is an inverted pyramid of biomass, found in aquatic (marine) ecosystems.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Explain the mode of action of contraceptive pills taken by human females. Mention the schedule to be followed for effective outcome.
questions.solution: Pills contain small doses of progestogens or progestogen-oestrogen combinations. They inhibit ovulation and implantation, and alter the quality of the cervical mucus to prevent or slow the entry of sperms. They are taken daily for 21 days, starting within the first five days of the menstrual cycle; after a gap of 7 days (when menstruation occurs) the course is repeated. (Saheli is taken once a week.)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Name and write two characteristics of the type of DNA that forms the basis of the DNA fingerprinting technique. (b) Mention any two applications of this technique.
questions.solution: (a) Repetitive DNA, especially VNTRs (variable number tandem repeats) in satellite DNA. They are highly polymorphic (the number of repeats differs between individuals), they are non-coding, and they are inherited. (b) Forensic identification of criminals, settling paternity disputes, and studying population and genetic diversity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Explain the significance of the experiment carried out by S.L. Miller. Name the scientists whose hypothesis prompted him to carry out this experiment. (b) How does meteorite analysis favour this hypothesis?
questions.solution: (a) Miller recreated early-Earth conditions in a closed flask with CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C, with electric discharges; amino acids were formed. This supported the chemical evolution of life from inorganic molecules proposed by Oparin and Haldane. (b) Meteorites contain similar organic compounds, showing that such processes also occur elsewhere in space.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Identify A to F : Pneumonia – Streptococcus – A; Typhoid – B – high fever, weakness, headache, stomach pain; Common cold – Rhino virus – C; Ringworm – D – dry scaly lesions, redness, itching; Ascariasis – Ascaris – E; F – Entamoeba histolytica – constipation, cramps, stools with mucous and blood clots.
questions.solution: A: fever, chills, cough, headache, and in severe cases grey-to-bluish lips and fingernails. B: Salmonella typhi. C: nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness. D: Microsporum, Trichophyton or Epidermophyton (fungi). E: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage. F: amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a family, the father, the daughter and the son are colour-blind, whereas the mother has normal vision. Do you think the son and the daughter have inherited the disease from their father? Work out a cross to justify your answer.
questions.solution: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. Father XᶜY; the mother must be a carrier XᶜX (since the daughter is affected). Cross XᶜX × XᶜY gives daughters XᶜXᶜ (colour-blind) and XᶜX (carrier), and sons XᶜY (colour-blind) and XY (normal). The daughter got one Xᶜ from her father and one from her mother. The son did not inherit it from his father (who gives him Y); his Xᶜ came from his mother.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) What are transgenic animals? (ii) Name the first transgenic cow and state its importance.
questions.solution: (i) Animals whose DNA has been manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene. (ii) Rosie (1997). It produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 g/L) containing human alpha-lactalbumin, which is nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Explain the convention for naming EcoRI. (ii) With the help of an illustration only, show the action of EcoRI on a DNA polynucleotide.
questions.solution: (i) E: genus Escherichia; co: species coli; R: strain RY13; I: the first enzyme isolated from that strain. (ii) 5′-G↓AATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAA↑G-5′: EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, giving 5′-G and AATTC-3′ fragments with single-stranded AATT overhangs (sticky ends).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Explain how it is ensured that the orchid Ophrys is pollinated by a specific species of bee. (b) Describe co-evolution with the help of this example.
questions.solution: (a) One petal of the Ophrys flower resembles the female bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee is attracted, 'pseudocopulates' with the petal and gets dusted with pollen, which it transfers when it visits another flower. (b) Plant and pollinator evolve together: if the female bee's colour pattern changes during evolution, pollination success drops unless the orchid's petal changes correspondingly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
India's land area is only 2.4 per cent of the world's total, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent; prokaryotes do not figure in these estimates. A survey of species richness of groups of mammals in three regions of the world is shown as a bar graph: taxonomic richness is lowest in Region I, higher in Region II and highest in Region III.

Why is the species richness maximum in Region III in the bar graph?
questions.solution: Region III is likely nearest the tropics: species diversity increases towards the equator because tropical regions have been less disturbed over geological time, have a less seasonal, more stable climate and receive more solar energy, so productivity is higher.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
India's land area is only 2.4 per cent of the world's total, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent; prokaryotes do not figure in these estimates. A survey of species richness of groups of mammals in three regions of the world is shown as a bar graph: taxonomic richness is lowest in Region I, higher in Region II and highest in Region III.

Why is the species richness minimum in Region I in the bar graph?
questions.solution: Region I is likely at a high latitude (towards the poles), where the harsh, seasonal climate and lower solar energy and productivity support fewer species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
India's land area is only 2.4 per cent of the world's total, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent; prokaryotes do not figure in these estimates. A survey of species richness of groups of mammals in three regions of the world is shown as a bar graph: taxonomic richness is lowest in Region I, higher in Region II and highest in Region III.

Plants and animals do not have uniform diversity in the world but show an uneven distribution. What is this kind of diversity referred to as?
questions.solution: The latitudinal gradient in diversity (a pattern of biodiversity).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
India's land area is only 2.4 per cent of the world's total, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent; prokaryotes do not figure in these estimates. A survey of species richness of groups of mammals in three regions of the world is shown as a bar graph: taxonomic richness is lowest in Region I, higher in Region II and highest in Region III.

Why do prokaryotes not have an estimated number of species as seen in plants and animals? Explain.
questions.solution: Conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species, and many cannot be cultured in the laboratory. Biochemical or molecular methods suggest their diversity runs into millions of species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A plasmid carries genes for ampicillin resistance and tetracycline resistance; foreign DNA is inserted into the tetracycline resistance gene to make recombinant DNA. After transformation, bacteria are grown on plate M, giving colonies 1 to 5. They are replica-plated onto plate N containing both tetracycline and ampicillin. On plate N, colonies 1, 2, 3 and 5 grow, but colony 4 does not.

Identify the colony that has been transformed with recombinant DNA. Justify your answer.
questions.solution: Colony 4. The insert has inactivated its tetracycline resistance gene (insertional inactivation), so it cannot grow on plate N with tetracycline, although it grew on plate M.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A plasmid carries genes for ampicillin resistance and tetracycline resistance; foreign DNA is inserted into the tetracycline resistance gene to make recombinant DNA. After transformation, bacteria are grown on plate M, giving colonies 1 to 5. They are replica-plated onto plate N containing both tetracycline and ampicillin. On plate N, colonies 1, 2, 3 and 5 grow, but colony 4 does not.

What are the sites in a plasmid called where the ampicillin and tetracycline resistance genes are present? State their role in genetic engineering.
questions.solution: Selectable markers. They help identify and select transformants from non-transformants: cells that take up the plasmid survive on the antibiotic, and insertion into one marker gene distinguishes recombinants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A plasmid carries genes for ampicillin resistance and tetracycline resistance; foreign DNA is inserted into the tetracycline resistance gene to make recombinant DNA. After transformation, bacteria are grown on plate M, giving colonies 1 to 5. They are replica-plated onto plate N containing both tetracycline and ampicillin. On plate N, colonies 1, 2, 3 and 5 grow, but colony 4 does not.

Name two enzymes playing an important role in genetic engineering.
questions.solution: Restriction endonuclease (molecular scissors) and DNA ligase (also DNA polymerase).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A plasmid carries genes for ampicillin resistance and tetracycline resistance; foreign DNA is inserted into the tetracycline resistance gene to make recombinant DNA. After transformation, bacteria are grown on plate M, giving colonies 1 to 5. They are replica-plated onto plate N containing both tetracycline and ampicillin. On plate N, colonies 1, 2, 3 and 5 grow, but colony 4 does not.

State the role of β-galactosidase in insertional inactivation.
questions.solution: When foreign DNA is inserted in the β-galactosidase gene, the enzyme is not made, so recombinant colonies stay white on a chromogenic substrate, while non-recombinants turn blue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Explain the development of the male gametophyte in an angiosperm. (ii) Draw a labelled diagram of a three-celled male gametophyte.
questions.solution: (i) Each microspore mother cell (pollen mother cell) in the anther undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of haploid microspores, which separate and develop into pollen grains. The pollen grain nucleus divides by mitosis into a large vegetative cell (with food reserve) and a small generative cell. In about 60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage; in the rest, the generative cell divides into two male gametes before shedding (3-celled stage). (ii) Labels: exine with germ pores, intine, vegetative cell with its nucleus, and two male gametes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Draw a diagrammatic sectional view of the ovary of a human female and label blood vessels, primary follicle, tertiary follicle and ovum. (ii) At which stage of life are primary follicles formed in a human female? (iii) Explain the events (both hormonal and structural) that occur from the time of ovulation till the onset of the next menstrual cycle.
questions.solution: (i) Section showing the stroma with blood vessels, primary follicles near the periphery, growing secondary and tertiary (antrum-containing) follicles, a Graafian follicle releasing the ovum, and the corpus luteum. (ii) Before birth, during foetal development. (iii) The LH surge causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum (ovulation). The remaining follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone that maintain the endometrium (secretory phase). If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium disintegrates, leading to menstruation and a new cycle.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Stability, one of the properties of genetic material, was very evident in one of the very early experiments in genetics. Name the scientist and describe his experiment. State the conclusion he arrived at.
questions.solution: Frederick Griffith (1928), with Streptococcus pneumoniae. S strain (smooth, capsulated) injected into mice killed them; R strain (rough) did not. Heat-killed S strain did not kill mice, but heat-killed S mixed with live R strain killed the mice, and live S bacteria were recovered from them. Conclusion: some 'transforming principle' from the heat-killed S strain transformed the R strain. The genetic material of the S strain survived heating unchanged, showing its stability.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A tall pea plant bearing violet flowers with unknown genotype is given. Find the genotype by working out different crosses only by selfing the plants. Write the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of each cross.
questions.solution: Self the plant and observe the progeny. (1) TTVV: all tall violet; genotype all TTVV. (2) TTVv: 3 tall violet : 1 tall white; genotypes 1 TTVV : 2 TTVv : 1 TTvv. (3) TtVV: 3 tall violet : 1 dwarf violet; genotypes 1 TTVV : 2 TtVV : 1 ttVV. (4) TtVv: 9 tall violet : 3 tall white : 3 dwarf violet : 1 dwarf white; genotypes 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 (TTVV, TTVv, TTvv, TtVV, TtVv, Ttvv, ttVV, ttVv, ttvv). The progeny pattern tells which genotype the plant has.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Name and explain the property present in normal cells but lost in cancer cells. (ii) All normal human cells have genes that may become cancerous under certain conditions. Name them and explain how. (iii) State the role of the following in detection and diagnosis of cancer : (1) Biopsy and histopathology (2) Magnetic resonance imaging
questions.solution: (i) Contact inhibition: in normal cells, contact with other cells stops further growth; cancer cells lose it and keep dividing into tumours. (ii) Proto-oncogenes (cellular oncogenes); under certain conditions such as mutation or carcinogens they become activated and cause oncogenic transformation. (iii)(1) A piece of the suspected tissue is cut into thin sections, stained and examined under a microscope by a pathologist. (2) MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In a sewage treatment plant, the primary effluent is passed into large aeration tanks, and the effluent is then passed into settling tanks to form a 'sediment'. (i) (1) Why is the primary effluent passed into large aeration tanks? (2) What is the sediment called? Mention its significance. (3) Explain the final step in the settling tank before the treated effluent is released into water bodies. (ii) Name any two organisms used as bio-fertilisers, belonging to different kingdoms. Write how each acts as a bio-fertiliser.
questions.solution: (i)(1) It is constantly agitated and air is pumped in, allowing vigorous growth of aerobic microbes as flocs (bacteria with fungal filaments) which consume the organic matter and reduce BOD. (2) Activated sludge. A small part is pumped back into the aeration tank as inoculum; the rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, where bacteria digest it and produce biogas. (3) The flocs settle, and the clear supernatant effluent, with much lower BOD, is released into rivers and streams. (ii) Rhizobium (bacteria): fixes atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules of legumes. Glomus (fungi): forms mycorrhiza and absorbs phosphorus from soil for the plant. (Anabaena, a cyanobacterium, also fixes nitrogen.)
